title: Four Lepers and a Day of Good News
summary: In besieged, starving Samaria, Elisha announces that by the next day flour and barley will sell cheaply at the city gate; the king's officer scoffs and is told he will see it but not eat it. That night four lepers outside the gate go over to the Aramean camp and find it deserted, because the LORD made the Arameans hear the sound of a great army. The lepers bring the news to the city, the people plunder the camp, prices fall exactly as Elisha said, and the scoffing officer is trampled to death in the gate.
story: Chapter 6 ended at the lowest point of the siege: mothers eating their children and the king vowing to kill Elisha, his messenger at the prophet's door, and the despairing cry, why wait for the LORD any longer. This chapter is the LORD's answer, and it comes in two parts: a word, and then its fulfillment down to the price of grain. The chapter completes the long Aramean war stories of chapters 5 through 7 and shows that the city was saved not by the king's army or strategy but by God acting alone, with four outcasts as his messengers. It also carries a warning in the officer's fate, since unbelief sees God's work without sharing in it.
historical:
The siege of Samaria by Ben-hadad belongs to the reign of an Omride king, probably Jehoram (about 852 to 841 BC), though the text does not name him. The Arameans fear that Israel has hired the kings of the Hittites and of Egypt (verse 6). In the ninth century BC the name Hittites referred not to the old Hittite empire of Anatolia, which had fallen centuries earlier, but to the Neo-Hittite kingdoms of northern Syria and southeastern Turkey, such as Carchemish and Hamath, which Assyrian texts also call the land of Hatti. Egypt was weaker than in earlier centuries but still a power that could hire out or send forces. A threat from north and south at once would have made the Aramean position around Samaria untenable, which gives their panic a certain logic.

The route of their flight, traced by the scouts as far as the Jordan (verse 15), shows the Arameans heading east toward Gilead and home to Damascus. Dry measures and prices in the chapter are concrete. A seah was a dry measure of several liters, and a shekel was a weight of silver, about eleven or twelve grams. A seah of fine flour for a shekel was an ordinary price, remarkable only in comparison with the famine prices of 6:25.
cultural:
Under Israel's law, people with serious skin disease had to live outside the camp or city (Leviticus 13:46; Numbers 5:2-3), which is why the four lepers are at the gate rather than inside the walls. They depended on what people brought them, and in a siege no one brought anything. Their reasoning in verses 3-4 is that of people with nothing left to lose. The city gate in ancient Israel was the center of public life: the place of trade, legal cases, and news. It is fitting that the market reopens there and that the officer, appointed to keep order in the gate, dies there.

The officer on whose arm the king leaned was a senior royal aide; the same phrase is used of Naaman's role beside his king in 5:18. His mocking reply, that even windows in heaven would not make it possible, alludes to the picture of heaven's floodgates or windows opening to send rain (Genesis 7:11) or blessing (Malachi 3:10). He means that nothing short of a miracle could change prices so quickly, and he is right, though not in the way he meant.
literary: The chapter is built as prophecy, reversal, and precise fulfillment. Elisha's word in verse 1, with its specific prices, is repeated in verse 16 as fulfilled and again in verse 18 as the narrator looks back. The officer's scoffing reply in verse 2 is quoted again in verse 19, and his death is told twice (verses 17 and 20). This repetition drives home that every detail came true. The middle of the chapter shifts to the lepers and follows them step by step as they reason, walk, eat, hide plunder, and then stop themselves. Their confession, “We are not doing what is right. Today is a day of good news” (verse 9), is the turning point. The king's suspicion of an ambush (verse 12) adds a last moment of doubt, and it is an unnamed servant's practical suggestion that finally opens the city to its deliverance. God never appears on stage; the narrator mentions only once, in verse 6, what he did.

outline.t: Elisha's promise and the officer's scorn
The lepers find the Aramean camp deserted
The good news reaches the king, and scouts confirm it
The people plunder the camp and the word is fulfilled

doctrines.note: God delivers the city without a battle, by a sound in the enemy's ears (verse 6). The Arameans are routed by nothing but his action, and the result matches his word to the price of barley.
The officer's unbelief does not stop God's promise; it only shuts him out of it. He sees the plenty with his own eyes and dies before he can eat, as Elisha said.
The lepers realize that silence would be sin: good news for the whole city cannot be kept for themselves (verse 9). Those who have found life have an obligation to tell those still starving.

words.note: Besorah, good news or tidings. The lepers call this a day of besorah. The word and its verb are used for news of victory and, in Isaiah, for the announcement that God reigns and has come to save his people (Isaiah 40:9; 52:7). The Greek translation of the Old Testament uses the word family from which the New Testament's word for gospel comes.

Arubbah, window or opening, used of the windows of heaven that opened in the flood (Genesis 7:11) and that God promises to open in blessing (Malachi 3:10). The officer uses it in mockery; the chapter shows that God did not need to open heaven's windows to provide bread, only to turn an army to flight.

Qol, sound or voice. The LORD made the Arameans hear the qol of chariots, horses, and a great army (verse 6). No army was there; the sound was enough. The same word is used for God's own voice in thunder, and here the sound of an imaginary host does what Israel's actual army could not.

christ: The lepers' cry, that this is a day of good news and they must not keep silent, has long been heard by Christians as a picture of the gospel's spread. The link is thematic, but it is close: the New Testament uses the same family of words for the good news of Jesus, and the first people to carry it are often outsiders and the unclean. When John the Baptist asked whether Jesus was the one to come, Jesus answered that lepers are cleansed and the poor have good news proclaimed to them (Luke 7:22). The contrast between the lepers and the officer also anticipates Jesus' warnings that those who seem nearest to the kingdom may miss it through unbelief while outcasts enter first (Matthew 21:31). And the pattern of a people saved by God's act alone, receiving what they did not fight for, is the pattern of grace the New Testament proclaims.
questions: The lepers said, “If we are silent and wait until morning light, our sin will overtake us.” What good news have you received that others around you are still waiting to hear?
The officer saw the plenty but never tasted it. How can a person be close to what God is doing and still miss it through unbelief?
God chose four outcasts to announce a city's rescue. What does that suggest about the kind of people God uses, and about how we should listen to people we are inclined to overlook?
